themes.title: VA negative opinions lost weight when thin
themes.summary: The Board gave little weight to VA opinions that skipped records, ignored the veteran's account, used wrong facts or gave no reasons.

examples.condition: Chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis
examples.bullet: Negative VA opinions lost weight when they skipped the theory, literature or full record.
Negative VA opinions lost weight when based on wrong facts or ignoring the veteran's account
A negative VA opinion lost weight when it leaned on silent service records.
Negative VA opinions that were conclusory or skipped key evidence lost weight.
VA negative opinions built on wrong facts or missed questions got little or no weight

themes.title: A reasoned doctor opinion linked it to service
themes.summary: Private or treating doctors who gave reasons, cited records or studies, and tied the condition to service carried weight with the Board.

examples.condition: Major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease
examples.bullet: Private doctor opinions that reviewed the file and cited medical studies got strong weight.
Board gave high weight to private opinions that cited medical studies and explained the link.
Favorable opinion giving a stated reason, such as service activity or medical literature, was credited.
Doctor opinions tying gastritis to NSAID use for service-connected conditions were accepted.
Private opinions with full record review and written reasoning drew significant weight from the Board.

themes.title: Credible personal accounts were accepted
themes.summary: The Board accepted believable accounts of symptoms that began in service and continued, especially when records fit the story.

examples.bullet: Credible veteran accounts of when joint symptoms began were accepted.
Credible personal account of eye problems since service, consistent with records, was accepted.

examples.condition: Disorders of the lacrimal apparatus (epiphora, dacryocystitis, etc.)
examples.bullet: Veteran's own report of dry eyes starting in service and continuing was accepted.
Consistent veteran accounts of back injury and pain since service were found credible

examples.condition: Crohn's disease or undifferentiated form of inflammatory bowel disease
examples.bullet: Credible accounts from the veteran and family of stomach symptoms in service and after helped.

themes.title: Sent back for a new exam or opinion
themes.summary: When VA gave no exam, or an exam that skipped a theory, a symptom or the records, the Board sent the claim back instead of deciding it.

examples.bullet: Sent back when the VA examiner ignored the veteran's account or gave no reasons.
Sent back for a new opinion when VA's opinion was conclusory or skipped a theory.
Sent back for new opinions when VA examiners skipped a secondary or direct theory.

examples.condition: Aortic aneurysm: Ascending, thoracic, or abdominal
examples.bullet: Sent back for an opinion when no examiner addressed a possible secondary link.

examples.condition: Erectile dysfunction, with or without penile deformity
examples.bullet: Claims were sent back when VA examiners did not address aggravation by a service-connected condition.

themes.title: Records from service showed the problem
themes.summary: Treatment notes, complaints or diagnoses recorded during service supported the in-service part of the claim.

examples.bullet: Service records showing foot or toe complaints or treatment supported the claim.
Eye injury or diagnosis recorded during service backed the later claim.
Service records showing gynecologic treatment during service supported the grants.
Service records showing a rash or eczema supported finding an in-service start.
Treatment records showing chest pain or costochondritis in service supported the claim.

themes.title: Secondary link to a service-connected condition
themes.summary: Medical opinions linking a new condition to one already service connected, by cause or by making it worse, supported secondary grants.

examples.bullet: A clinician tied glaucoma to a service-connected condition or its treatment.
A heart attack tied to a service-connected mental health condition or hypertension was granted.
Panic disorder was granted as secondary to another condition when the evidence was balanced.
Anemia tied by a medical opinion to a service-connected kidney or blood condition

examples.condition: Index or long finger, limitation of motion
examples.bullet: Reasoned opinions tying finger or thumb problems to duties or a service-connected condition carried weight.

themes.title: Exposure was conceded or presumed
themes.summary: Where service location or records supported exposure to herbicides, burn pits or similar hazards, the Board accepted exposure and the case turned on the medical link.

examples.bullet: Verified Southwest Asia service plus a current rhinitis diagnosis supported presumptive service connection

examples.condition: Malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system
examples.bullet: Credible accounts of work near a base perimeter or the DMZ established exposure.
Conceded or presumed herbicide exposure, from service location or a VA memo, supported the claim.
Conceded Gulf region service or toxic exposure supported grants of lung disease.
Board linked thyroid disease to conceded herbicide or toxic exposure when medical evidence supported it.

themes.title: Close evidence went to the veteran
themes.summary: When medical opinions or records were evenly balanced, the Board gave the veteran the benefit of the doubt.

examples.bullet: Evidence on stroke cause found evenly balanced, so doubt went to the veteran
Positive medical opinions balanced the evidence, and doubt was resolved for the veteran.
Competing medical opinions left the Board at even balance, and the claim was granted.
Favorable medical opinions, private or VA, supported grants, including when opinions were evenly balanced.

examples.condition: Tarsal, or metatarsal bones, malunion of, or nonunion of
examples.bullet: Positive opinions with reasoning, or split opinions, put foot claims in balance.

themes.title: Exams that missed flare-ups or pain were faulted
themes.summary: Exams that left out flare-ups, repeated use or medication effects were found inadequate, and many of those claims were sent back for a new exam.

examples.condition: Index or long finger, limitation of motion
examples.bullet: Sent back for a new exam when it missed flare-up or medication effects.
Sent back for a new exam when the examiner skipped flare-ups, bleeding or medication effects.
Exams missing weight-bearing, passive or flare-up testing were inadequate; some claims sent back.
Back exams that ignored flare-ups or repeated-use effects were sent back for a new exam
Exams missing flare-up findings were found inadequate and the claim was sent back.

themes.title: A current diagnosis was confirmed
themes.summary: An exam, treatment record or private diagnosis showing the condition during the claim met the current-disability question.

examples.bullet: A diagnosis in a VA exam or treatment record met the current-condition question.
A skin exam or treatment record naming alopecia met the current-disability question.
Diagnosis shown by lab tests, records or a VA exam met the current disability element.
A formal OCD diagnosis from a licensed clinician met the current-disability requirement.
A VA exam confirming lipomas or keratosis established the current diagnosis.

themes.title: Service records were silent
themes.summary: Records from service that showed no complaint, injury or diagnosis, or a normal separation exam, weighed against the claim.

examples.bullet: Service treatment records silent on thyroid problems weighed against the claim.
Service records with no GERD complaint or diagnosis weighed against a link.
Quiet service records and a clean separation exam weighed against in-service shin injury.
Service records silent on anemia, with first diagnosis years after discharge
Service treatment records and separation exam said nothing about the hips

themes.title: No current diagnosis was found
themes.summary: Exams and records that showed no diagnosis during the claim period ended the claim at the first step.

examples.bullet: Records with no diagnosis of a tendon condition left the claim without a current disability.
Claims failed where VA exams or records showed no vertigo diagnosis, despite dizziness complaints.
No current diagnosis of cold injury residuals in exams or records
No current hemorrhoid diagnosis in treatment records or exams ended the service claim.
No current rhinitis diagnosis in the records ended the service connection claim

themes.title: The veteran's own belief was not enough
themes.summary: Personal views on diagnosis or cause were not accepted as medical evidence, because those are medical questions.

examples.bullet: The veteran's own view that service caused the ringing was not accepted
The veteran's own view of the liver cause carried little weight without medical backing.
The veteran's own belief about the cause of migraines was not accepted as medical proof
A veteran's own belief about foot diagnosis or cause got little weight against medical evidence.

examples.condition: Major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease
examples.bullet: Veteran or family belief that service caused dementia was not competent evidence of cause.

themes.title: Years passed before the first diagnosis or care
themes.summary: Long gaps between service and the first complaint, treatment or diagnosis weighed against a link to service.

examples.bullet: Long gaps between service and first back treatment weighed against a link to service
Silent service records and respiratory records first appearing decades later weighed against the claim.
Heart disease first diagnosed decades after service, with silent service records, weighed against the claim.
Arthritis first appearing in records decades after service weighed against the claim.
A first diagnosis long after service, with normal earlier records, weakened the claim.

themes.title: Reasoned VA opinions against a link carried weight
themes.summary: VA opinions that reviewed the file and explained why the condition was not linked to service outweighed competing views.

examples.bullet: Negative VA opinions citing medical literature and other stroke risk factors were given high weight
A negative VA opinion with clear reasons, often a long smoking history, was adopted.
Negative VA opinions with explained reasoning were found probative against a service link.

examples.condition: Malignant skin neoplasms (other than malignant melanoma)
examples.bullet: Negative VA opinions with a rationale, literature and an accurate history were found persuasive.
Explained negative VA opinion with no opposing medical opinion weighed against the claim

themes.title: No doctor tied it to service
themes.summary: Without a medical opinion linking the condition or exposure to service, the link was left unsupported.

examples.condition: Chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis
examples.bullet: No medical opinion linking kidney disease to service left direct claims unsupported.
Board found no medical opinion or evidence linking melanoma to the reported exposure.
Conceded herbicide or toxic exposure did not carry the claim without a medical link
No medical opinion tied HIV to service, so the claim fell short.
No medical opinion linked the eye disease to service.

themes.title: The claimed exposure was not shown
themes.summary: Records that did not place the veteran in a covered place, or did not confirm the exposure, left the exposure theory unproven.

examples.bullet: Herbicide exposure was not accepted when service location or dates fell outside the presumption.

examples.condition: Malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system
examples.bullet: Service outside the listed places and periods meant exposure was not presumed.
Herbicide exposure stayed unproven when records showed no service in a listed location.
Records did not show herbicide exposure, so the heart claim failed on that theory.
Herbicide or toxic exposure claimed for a stroke was not shown by the record.

themes.title: Opinions without reasons got little weight
themes.summary: Opinions, letters or notes with no stated reasons, no record review or no clinical findings were given little or no weight.

examples.bullet: A private opinion with no stated reasons or no examination carried little weight

examples.condition: Aortic aneurysm: Ascending, thoracic, or abdominal
examples.bullet: Private opinions without full reasoning were found inadequate or given no weight.
Favorable opinions with no rationale, or built on the veteran account alone, were discounted.
Private opinions got little weight when they lacked reasoning or skipped the period at issue.
A positive opinion with no explanation, or built on general articles, got little weight

themes.title: Earlier records contradicted the veteran's account
themes.summary: Accounts of continuous symptoms lost weight when older records, separation paperwork or earlier histories said something different.

examples.bullet: Later claims of constant pain were not believed when older records said otherwise
Later claims of foot symptoms since service lost credibility when earlier histories said otherwise.
Claims of pain since service lost weight when contemporaneous records showed no back complaints
Separation paperwork where the veteran denied ear trouble was weighed against the claim
A veteran's account of in-service onset was outweighed when records did not corroborate it
